Boron is essential to plant growth, but water soluble levels in excess of 5-10 parts per million (ppm) can be toxic to plants. Boron levels exceeding 5 ppm were identified in 25 intervals from eight holes on Tract III and seven intervals from three holes on Tract II. In most cases the boron concentration was less than 10 ppm, with values higher than 10 occurring in 12 samples. Except for a coal interval with 138 ppm, the highest value encountered was 22 ppm. High boron levels were most often eacountered in the overburden. Overburden mixing should dilute boron concentrations to acceptable levels, but the possibility exists that boron levels in excess of 5 ppm may occasionally occur at the surface of regraded spoils.
Molybdenum is of concern because although it is an essential micronutrient, high levels in forage plants can be detrimental to livestock through interference with copper. Nearly all intervals tested had molybdenum levels below 1.0 ppm, and in no cases were critical levels approached.
Potential problems due to excessive levels of iron, copper or manganese were not indicated.
Trace Elements - Trace elements are those not essential for plant growth, but which may be toxic to plants or animals when accumulated or ingested in excessive amounts. The highest level of mercury encountered was less than 600 parts per billion (ppb), with most levels less than 100 ppb. These values are within the range normally encountered in surface soils.
